history.heading: Putnam’s, 1853
paragraphs: “Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall-Street” appeared without Melville’s name in *Putnam’s Monthly Magazine*, in two parts, in the November and December issues of 1853. *Moby-Dick* (1851) and *Pierre* (1852) had sold badly and left him in debt to his publishers, Harper and Brothers.
In May 1856 Dix and Edwards of New York reprinted the story, with small changes to the text, in *The Piazza Tales*, this time under Melville’s name.

history.heading: Poems, 1920
paragraphs: Wilfred Owen was born near Oswestry on 18 March 1893 and was killed on 4 November 1918, during the crossing of the Sambre–Oise Canal, a week before the Armistice. His mother received the telegram on Armistice Day, while the church bells in Shrewsbury were ringing.

Only five of his poems were published in his lifetime. He had met Siegfried Sassoon at Craiglockhart War Hospital in Edinburgh, where both were patients, and Sassoon, with help from Edith Sitwell, edited *Poems* and wrote its introduction. Chatto and Windus published it in 1920. The book had twenty-three poems and the unfinished Preface found among Owen’s papers: “My subject is War, and the pity of War. The Poetry is in the pity.”
Edmund Blunden’s edition of 1931 added nineteen more.

history.heading: Nine years to publication
paragraphs: Joyce’s first published fiction was an early version of “The Sisters”, printed in *The Irish Homestead* on 13 August 1904 under the name Stephen Daedalus. Versions of “Eveline” and “After the Race” followed in the same paper before the end of the year.

Grant Richards agreed to publish the collection in 1905. His printer refused to set “Two Gallants”, Richards asked for further cuts, and when Joyce agreed to only some of them Richards withdrew. Maunsel and Company of Dublin signed a contract in 1909 and had the book set in type, but its managing director, George Roberts, objected to the real people and places named in it and would not publish. In 1912 the printer destroyed the sheets. Joyce kept a set of proofs, and on the journey back from Dublin wrote a broadside in verse against Roberts, “Gas from a Burner”.
Grant Richards finally published *Dubliners* on 15 June 1914, setting it from the Maunsel proofs. Joyce had submitted the book eighteen times to fifteen publishers.

history.heading: Vienna, London and the ending
paragraphs: Shaw wrote *Pygmalion* early in 1912 and read it to Mrs Patrick Campbell that June. Its first performance was in German, in Siegfried Trebitsch’s translation, at the Hofburg Theatre in Vienna on 16 October 1913. The London production opened at His Majesty’s Theatre on 11 April 1914, with Herbert Beerbohm Tree as Higgins and Mrs Patrick Campbell as Eliza, and ran for 118 performances.
Shaw was irritated by the romantic ending Tree gave the play, and when it was published in 1916 he added a prose sequel, “What Happened Afterwards”, to settle what becomes of Eliza.

For the 1938 film, with Leslie Howard and Wendy Hiller, Shaw wrote new scenes, and he shared the Academy Award for its screenplay. Some of those scenes went into the printed play in 1941. This edition prints the 1916 text, without them.

history.heading: Talland House and Skye
paragraphs: The Hogarth Press, run by Virginia and Leonard Woolf, published *To the Lighthouse* on 5 May 1927 in a first printing of 3,000 copies; Harcourt Brace published it in New York the same year. It won the Prix Femina–Vie Heureuse in 1928.

The novel is in three parts, “The Window”, “Time Passes” and “The Lighthouse”, and is set at the Ramsays’ summer house on the Isle of Skye. Behind it is Talland House in St Ives, Cornwall, which Woolf’s father, Leslie Stephen, rented for the family’s summers from 1882. Her mother died when Woolf was thirteen. Her sister, Vanessa Bell, told her that reading the book was like seeing their mother “raised from the dead”.

history.heading: Keats’s last book
paragraphs: Taylor and Hessey announced *Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems* on 26 June 1820, and its publication is usually dated 1 July. It was the third and last book of poems Keats published, and it printed “To Autumn”, “Ode to Psyche”, “Ode on Melancholy” and “Hyperion” for the first time.

The publishers put an Advertisement at the front, saying that “Hyperion” had been left unfinished because the reception of *Endymion* had discouraged its author. Keats had not written it, and in one copy he crossed it out and wrote “This is a lie”.
By then he was seriously ill with tuberculosis. He sailed for Italy with Joseph Severn in September 1820 and died in Rome on 23 February 1821.

history.heading: Thoor Ballylee
paragraphs: Macmillan published *The Tower* in London in 1928. It was Yeats’s first major collection since the Nobel Prize of 1923, and its twenty-one poems include “Sailing to Byzantium”, “Leda and the Swan”, “Among School Children”, “Meditations in Time of Civil War” and “Nineteen Hundred and Nineteen”.

The tower of the title is Thoor Ballylee, the Norman tower in County Galway that Yeats bought in 1917 and restored. Thomas Sturge Moore’s design for the cover, stamped in gold on green cloth, shows the tower reflected in the water below it.

history.heading: A best-seller and its critics
paragraphs: Claude McKay was born in Jamaica and was known as a poet, for *Harlem Shadows* among other books, when he wrote *Home to Harlem*, his first novel, during the years he spent in Europe and North Africa. Harper and Brothers published it in 1928, and it became a best-seller.

Not everyone welcomed it. W. E. B. Du Bois reviewed it in *The Crisis* in June 1928, alongside Nella Larsen’s *Quicksand*, and wrote that it “for the most part nauseates me, and after the dirtier parts of its filth I feel distinctly like taking a bath.” In 1929 McKay received the Harmon Foundation’s gold award for literature.
